timeline.title: Izel on the Reims-Trier Roman road
timeline.text: The great Roman road known as the “Brunehaut” linked Reims with Trier via Mouzon, Carignan, Izel, Bellefontaine and Arlon. From Izel, another road led to Chiny, roughly following today's road. The name Izel is said to be of Celtic origin and to mean “low”, but this etymology is not sourced.

timeline.title: The “Brunehaut tower” and the little temple at Pin
timeline.text: In the 17th century, Alexandre Wiltheim, regarded as the first Luxembourg archaeologist, described a ruined octagonal tower near Pin beside the Roman road. In the late 1970s, the National Excavation Service found no trace of it. It did, however, uncover a Roman-era settlement and a small temple (fanum), with pottery, bas-reliefs, wall decorations and a bronze statuette of Eros.

timeline.title: The County of Chiny
timeline.text: The County of Chiny emerged in the late 10th century as a dependency of the County of Bar. At its height, it covered the south of the Ardennes, most of the Gaume and part of the Chiers valley. The counts' fortified castle stood on a rocky spur overlooking the Semois at Chiny; only a few remains survive. Izel was part of this territory.

timeline.title: Annexation to the Duchy of Luxembourg
timeline.text: After four centuries of prosperity, the County of Chiny was annexed to the Duchy of Luxembourg in 1364. Some sources give 1365. Like the rest of Luxembourg, the region then passed to the Dukes of Burgundy, and later to the Spanish and Austrian Habsburgs.

timeline.title: The Black Death in the Gaume
timeline.text: In 1636, in the midst of the Thirty Years' War, plague struck the region and literally wiped several hamlets off the map. At Frenois, a calvary erected as an ex-voto to Our Lady of Luxembourg recalls the epidemic. Nothing specific has been found about Izel itself during this period.

timeline.title: The Du Mont castle in Izel
timeline.text: In the 17th century, the Du Mont family (also Dumont or Del Monte) had a castle built in Izel. Its gateway survives, carved with the family coat of arms (three martlets, birds with neither feet nor beak) and the date 1675. The gateway stands opposite the Athénée royal d'Izel (secondary school).

timeline.title: French Revolution, then the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg, then Belgium
timeline.text: The region was annexed by France in 1795; Luxembourg then became the Département des Forêts. In 1815 it joined the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg, united with the Kingdom of the Netherlands. In 1823, the neighbouring municipality of Moyen was merged with Izel. Under the Treaty of London of 1839, the Gaume left the Grand Duchy and became part of the new Belgian province of Luxembourg.

timeline.title: Izel railway station opens
timeline.text: On 20 December 1880, the Belgian State opened the Florenville-Bertrix section of the Athus-Meuse line (line 165), with a station at Izel. It lay between the Jamoigne and Pin stops, at the highest point of the Virton-Florenville stretch. The station closed to passengers on 3 June 1984; the building is now a private home, and trains still pass through without stopping.

timeline.title: The Marbehan - Sainte-Cécile light railway tram
timeline.text: In 1911, a non-electrified metre-gauge light railway tram linked Marbehan with Sainte-Cécile via Jamoigne and Florenville. The municipal brochure numbers it line 163, Wikipedia line 558. It transformed village life by making it easier to travel, send post and transport goods. In May 1940, army engineers blew up all the bridges to slow the German advance, and the line never reopened. Its former route is now a walking path (RAVeL) along the Semois.

timeline.title: Lieutenant de Crépy, at Les Bulles
timeline.text: Baron Jean de Crépy, a lieutenant in the French 4th Hussars, was wounded during a reconnaissance and then killed by German dragoons on 15 August 1914. A monument marks the spot at Les Bulles, about 3.5 km from Izel. The lieutenant is buried in Les Bulles cemetery, and his horse at the site of the ambush.

timeline.title: Battle of Rossignol and the Tintigny massacre
timeline.text: On 22 August 1914, during the Battle of the Frontiers, the French 3rd Colonial Infantry Division was wiped out in the forest of Rossignol, about 9 km east of Izel. On the same day, around three quarters of Tintigny was burned (183 houses) and 63 inhabitants were killed, falsely accused of being francs-tireurs (irregular snipers). German Regiments 38 and 51 have been held responsible.

timeline.title: Moyen, Izel and Pin set on fire
timeline.text: On the morning of 23 August, the Germans defeated the French colonial troops at Les Bulles. During the night, their scouts reached Moyen. From 5 a.m. on 24 August, Moyen was set on fire and its inhabitants were forced at bayonet point to set fire to their own houses. The troops then crossed the Semois and entered Izel. Most of its 650 inhabitants had fled: 8 civilians were killed, but 54 or 55 houses were burned. The figures given are 7 killed and 58 houses in Moyen, and 5 killed and 49 houses in Pin.

timeline.title: The Rossignol civilians shot at Arlon
timeline.text: After the battle, the Germans deported around 120 inhabitants of Rossignol and the neighbouring villages, then shot them at Arlon on 26 August 1914, near the railway station. Depending on the source, there were between 120 and 125 victims. At Rossignol, the “caveau des fusillés” (vault of the executed) and several monuments commemorate this tragedy.

timeline.title: The Harmonie Caecilia is founded
timeline.text: The Royal Harmonie Caecilia of Izel, a wind band, was founded in 1920. In 2007 it rose to the first division of the Music Federation of Belgian Luxembourg. For a time it used the old village wash house, as the small lyre fixed to the pediment recalls.

timeline.title: The invasion of May 1940
timeline.text: During the Battle of France, Izel was taken on 12 May 1940 by the German 36th Infantry Division, according to Jean-Yves Mary (Le Corridor des Panzers, 2009). As they withdrew, the Allied troops blew up the bridges: the tram bridge and the Saint-Nicolas stone bridge at Chiny, rebuilt identically in 1959.

timeline.title: The Jewish children hidden at the Château du Faing (Jamoigne)
timeline.text: During the Occupation, the “Home Reine Élisabeth”, housed in the Château du Faing at Jamoigne, 2.5 km from Izel, hid Jewish children among its boarders. Yad Vashem counts 83 of them, the municipality 87. The director Marie Taquet-Mertens, her husband Émile and other members of staff were recognised as Righteous Among the Nations; a plaque commemorates this. The château now houses the municipal offices of Chiny.

timeline.title: The Liberation
timeline.text: The US 28th Infantry Division, nicknamed the “Bloody Bucket”, entered Belgium on 7 September 1944 through the Muno sector, south-west of Florenville. It liberated the south of the province: Virton on 9 September, Arlon on 10 September. No source has been found for the exact date of Izel's liberation, most likely between 7 and 10 September 1944. In the Moyen woods, the Notre-Dame du Maquis monument commemorates the local Resistance fighters.

timeline.title: Izel becomes part of Chiny
timeline.text: Previously an independent municipality, Izel, which also included Moyen, Pin and Laneuville, was merged on 1 January 1977 into the new municipality of Chiny, together with Chiny, Jamoigne, Les Bulles, Suxy and Termes. The section (former municipality) had 1,865 inhabitants on 1 January 2025.

sites.name: St Peter's Church, Izel
sites.text: The village parish church, next to the cemetery. Its dedication to St Peter is given by the Dutch Wikipedia and by OpenStreetMap. No construction date or history has been found; it remains to be checked whether it was affected by the fire of 24 August 1914.

sites.name: Izel cemetery and war memorials
sites.text: According to TracesOfWar, the Izel war memorial is topped by a soldier leaning on his rifle. It bears the dates 1914-1918 and a 1940-1945 panel with 12 names. The cemetery also has a First World War monument and, on the wall, a very worn plaque with almost illegible names. The exact location of the main memorial has not been verified; the coordinates given are those of the cemetery.

sites.name: Gateway of the Du Mont castle (1675)
sites.text: The only remnant of the castle built in the 17th century by the Du Mont family. The gateway bears the family coat of arms, three martlets, and the date 1675. It marks the car park exit, opposite the Athénée royal d'Izel, rue des Quatre Vents. The coordinates are those of the Athénée, so they are approximate.

sites.name: Old wash house, Izel
sites.text: A neoclassical wash house, described as one of the finest in the region. The Harmonie Caecilia used it for a time, hence the small lyre on the pediment. The municipality places it at the junction of rue du Lavoir and rue de l'Auwy; the coordinates are those of this junction, on the Pin side. Note: OpenStreetMap also shows a historic wash house in the centre of Izel (49.69382, 5.37579). To be checked on site.

sites.name: Former Izel station and the “pig bridge”
sites.text: Station on line 165 (Athus-Meuse), in service from 1880 to 1984, rue de la Gare, at 361 m above sea level. The building is now a private house: view it from the street. Close by, on the GR footpath, a small bridge passes under the track: this is the “pont des cochons” (pig bridge), through which farmers drove their pigs to forage in the forest.

sites.name: Former light railway tram route (RAVeL, chemin du Brugeland)
sites.text: The trackbed of the old Marbehan - Sainte-Cécile tram (1911-1940) has become a walking and cycling path. It follows the Semois between Izel and Jamoigne, then heads towards Florenville. In Jamoigne, the route is waymarked behind the sports centre.

sites.name: St Walfroy's Church, Pin
sites.text: The church of the hamlet of Pin, 1 km south of Izel; Pin is part of the Izel section. Its dedication comes from OpenStreetMap; no date or history has been found. Pin was burned on 24 August 1914: 49 houses destroyed, 5 civilians killed.

sites.name: Gallo-Roman site of the “Brunehaut tower” (Pin)
sites.text: An octagonal tower once stood here, described in the 17th century by Wiltheim beside the Roman road. Excavations in the late 1970s revealed a settlement and a fanum, a small Roman temple. Almost nothing is visible today. The exact location has not been found.

sites.name: Moyen: the Pâquis footbridge and the bridge over the Semois
sites.text: Moyen lies directly opposite Izel, on the other bank of the Semois. When the river floods, several times a year, people cross on foot by the Pâquis footbridge, near the main bridge. On 24 August 1914, the inhabitants here were forced to burn their own houses.

sites.name: Notre-Dame du Maquis (Buneau wood, Moyen)
sites.text: At the edge of the Buneau wood, this monument commemorates the Resistance fighters of the Second World War. Close by, the pont de Fer (iron bridge) crosses the Vierre between Moyen and Suxy: it is an old metal bridge salvaged from the SNCB (Belgian railways), once used by the workers of the Croisettes estate. The coordinates have not been found, and the Resistance group honoured has not been identified.

sites.name: Château du Faing (Jamoigne)
sites.text: This was the former seigneury of the du Faing family; Gilles du Faing was made a baron by the King of Spain in 1623. The Count of Loen demolished it and rebuilt it in Gothic Revival style after 1872, scattering the raven from his coat of arms all over it. A Red Cross hospital in 1914-1918, then a refuge for more than 80 Jewish children in 1942-1944. It is now Chiny town hall, with a commemorative plaque.

sites.name: St Peter's Church, Jamoigne
sites.text: It was probably built in the 11th century on the ruins of the Carolingian estate of “Gammunias”, which explains its isolated position on a mound. The old altar rests on a fragment of a Roman column decorated with vines. Inside are the carved portraits of Jean du Faing and Françoise de Cugnon.

sites.name: Lieutenant de Crépy monument (Les Bulles)
sites.text: A memorial stone to Baron Jean de Crépy, a lieutenant in the 4th Hussars, killed on 15 August 1914 by German dragoons during a reconnaissance. He was one of the very first to die in the war in the region.

sites.name: Notre-Dame de la Chavée
sites.text: A large Virgin and Child several metres high, on a mound reached by two flights of steps, at the crossroads of Romponcelle, Jamoigne, Prouvy and Valansart.

sites.name: Saint-Nicolas bridge and the Fort quarter (Chiny)
sites.text: The first bridge, made of wood, dates from the time of the counts. The stone bridge that replaced it was destroyed during the Second World War, then rebuilt identically in 1959; St Nicholas appears on it as patron saint of boatmen. In the upper part of the town, rue du Fort, rue du Donjon and chemin des Remparts recall the stronghold of the Counts of Chiny. It is also the starting point for boat trips down the Semois.

sites.name: French military cemetery of l'Orée de la Forêt (Rossignol)
sites.text: A cemetery for the colonial soldiers who fell on 22 August 1914; other monuments are close by. Here you will find the memorial stone of the writer Ernest Psichari, grandson of Renan, killed at Rossignol, as well as the “caveau des fusillés” (vault of the executed) (49.71543, 5.48548) for the civilians executed at Arlon.

sites.name: Orval Abbey
sites.text: About 6 km south of Izel (municipality of Florenville): the ruins of the medieval Cistercian abbey, the abbey rebuilt in the 20th century and the Mathilde fountain, birthplace of the legend of the trout and the ring. The coordinates are approximate.

legends.title: The trout and Mathilde's ring (Orval)
legends.text: A widowed countess, Mathilde, often identified as Matilda of Tuscany or of Canossa, dropped her wedding ring into a spring. She prayed, and a trout rose to the surface with the ring in its mouth. The countess exclaimed that this place was truly a “val d'or”, a golden valley: this is said to be the origin of the name Orval. Out of gratitude, she is said to have supported the founding of the monastery. The trout with the ring still appears on the abbey's coat of arms and on the Orval beer label.

legends.title: The lady who saved her husband (Château de la Cour, between Florenville and Martué)
legends.text: According to a legend recorded in 1920, a Count of Chiny laid a long siege to this castle. Before destroying it, he allowed the lady of the castle to leave, taking with her “what she held most precious”. She then hoisted her husband onto her back and crossed the lines. The count, outwitted but true to his word, had to let her pass. The author points out that the history of Chiny in no way confirms this tale.

legends.title: The Fairies' Hole at Chassepierre
legends.text: Tradition has it that Chassepierre was founded by a fisherman who lived in a cave hollowed out of the rock, the “casa petra”, from which the village's name is said to come. The cave became the Trou des Fées (Fairies' Hole): at night the fairies came out to dance in the meadow opposite, which bears the sinister name “Marc de Sang”. It was also said that a tunnel connected it to the castle, or even all the way to Carignan.

legends.title: The Jacob cross (Les Bulles)
legends.text: It is said that a scrap-metal dealer, Jean-Baptiste Jacob, found a cast-iron cross in his day's haul. Rather than melt it down with the old iron, he fixed it to a tree at the edge of the wood, on the Blofagnu path. The spot has kept the name “croix Jacob” (Jacob's cross) ever since.

legends.title: The Roche du Corbeau (Chiny)
legends.text: It is said that the “real” Roche du Corbeau (Raven's Rock) lay a little further on, towards the Saint-Nicolas bridge. Once that rock was overgrown, the name supposedly shifted to the one pointed out today. Another explanation derives the name from the Old French “recorbeillé”, meaning curved back.

legends.title: Gaumais, the local language
legends.text: Gaumais is a variety of Romance Lorrain, a langue d'oïl. It has been recognised by the Wallonia-Brussels Federation as an indigenous regional language since 1990, but it is now seriously endangered: the number of speakers is estimated at around 5,000. A few words: “crombîre” (potato), “waffe” (waffle). “Tchantans, tchantans” is one of the best-known Gaumais songs, and a mass is celebrated in Gaumais every year at Tintigny. The people of Izel are called Izelois; those of Pin, Pinots; those of Moyen, Moyins; and those of Chiny, Tchinots.

legends.title: The Chiny Intercultural Storytelling Festival
legends.text: Founded in 1990, it is the second-oldest storytelling festival in the French-speaking world, after the one in Grenoble. Every year around mid-July, it takes over the streets of Chiny with performances, young storytellers' competitions and evenings around the fire. Izel, for its part, is known for its Fête de la musique.

culture.title: Gaumais, a Lorrain dialect
culture.text: In the Gaume, people do not speak Walloon: the local dialect, Gaumais, is a variety of Romance Lorrain, a langue d'oïl close to French. It is recognised as an indigenous regional language by the Wallonia-Brussels Federation, but UNESCO classes it as “severely endangered” (2010). A few local authors are trying to revive it.

culture.title: “Belgium's little Provence”
culture.text: The Gaume (Belgian Lorraine) is nicknamed “Belgium's little Provence” because its climate is milder than that of the neighbouring Ardennes. This is what allows vines to grow at Torgny and the Plate de Florenville potato to be cultivated on sandy limestone soils. It is also called the “little Midi of Belgium”, but no source with figures on the microclimate has been found.

culture.title: Gaume Nature Park
culture.text: A nature park created by decree of the Walloon Government of 18 December 2014, covering around 58,100 ha. It protects the biodiversity and heritage of the Gaume: landscapes, architecture, small-scale heritage and culture. Its municipalities are Étalle, Florenville, Meix-devant-Virton, Musson, Rouvroy, Saint-Léger, Tintigny, Virton and part of Aubange. Chiny does not appear in the lists consulted.

culture.title: The Gaume house and its usoir
culture.text: Gaume villages have a consistent layout, architecture and colour scheme: terraced 19th-century rural houses whose doors and windows show the use of each part (living quarters, barn, cowshed). In front of the façade lies the usoir, an open space typical of Lorraine that the Nature Park recommends leaving unfenced. The details of the historical use of the usoir have not been verified.

culture.title: Chiny, City of Tales
culture.text: Chiny, the former capital of the powerful County of Chiny (founded around 980), has given itself the title of “Cité des contes” (City of Tales). Every year, on the second weekend of July, the Intercultural Storytelling Festival makes the small town pedestrian-only and brings together some sixty storytellers, with storytelling walks, a Night of Tales and workshops. The number of editions varies between sources.

culture.title: The Semois boatmen and the legends of the rocks
culture.text: For a century, flat-bottomed boats have been taking visitors down the Semois from Chiny to Lacuisine (about 8 km, one hour) through the Hât gorge. The boatman tells the legends of the rocks and riverbanks, such as the Trou du Diable (Devil's Hole) and the Roche aux Fées (Fairies' Rock). A recent guide suggests the service has been reduced: call the Passeurs réunis (+32 61 31 17 43) before counting on it. Kayaks, on the other hand, run well.

culture.title: Rocher du Hat
culture.text: A viewpoint over a meander of the Semois, described as the highest point on the Semois (365 m) between Chiny and Lacuisine. It is a classic walk from Chiny.

culture.title: Orval, the abbey and the legend of the trout
culture.text: According to legend, the widowed Countess Mathilde lost her wedding ring in a spring in the valley. A trout brought it back to her and she exclaimed: “This is truly a Val d'Or (golden valley)!”, then vowed to found a monastery there. Cistercian from 1132, the abbey was burned in 1637 and rebuilt in the 20th century; monks still live there. Visitors can see the medieval ruins, the museum in the 18th-century cellars, the medicinal herb garden and the old pharmacy (allow 1.5 to 2 hours). The trout with the ring adorns the beer and the cheese.

culture.title: Chassepierre and its street arts festival
culture.text: Chassepierre, a village perched in a loop of the Semois with its church on the rock, its wash house and its mill, is one of the Most Beautiful Villages of Wallonia. Every mid-August it hosts the International Street Arts Festival, one of the pioneers of the genre in Europe: first held in 1974, its 52nd edition is in 2026.

culture.title: Gaume Jazz Festival
culture.text: A festival created in 1985 by the Jeunesses musicales of Belgian Luxembourg. It takes place every second weekend of August in the grounds of the Rossignol-Tintigny Cultural Centre (marquees, amphitheatre, church), with around twenty concerts. There are also spring, autumn and winter “Gaume Jazz” editions, and a workshop for young musicians. Rossignol is about 8 km from Izel.

culture.title: Musée gaumais (Virton)
culture.text: Housed since 1939 in the former Recollect friary in Virton, it tells two thousand years of Gaume history: archaeology, ironwork (fireplace firebacks), and folk arts and traditions. It also runs the Museum of Rural Life at Montquintin (a tithe farm from 1765, an old-fashioned classroom) and the lapidary museum at Montauban.

culture.title: Montauban-Buzenol: the Treveri harvester and contemporary art
culture.text: This fortified site, occupied in the Iron Age, the Gallo-Roman period and the Middle Ages, has yielded Gallo-Roman bas-reliefs, including the famous “Treveri harvester” (the vallus, the harvesting machine of the Gauls described by Pliny). They are displayed in an underground lapidary museum designed by the architect Constantin Brodzki. Since 2007, the Contemporary Art Centre of Belgian Luxembourg (CACLB) has held exhibitions on the site. A 6 km loop walk goes all round it. It is not known whether the original harvester is at Montauban or in Virton.

culture.title: Chameleux Gallo-Roman site
culture.text: Remains of a Roman roadside staging post on the Reims-Trier road, occupied from the 1st to the 5th century, a few kilometres from Florenville.

culture.title: Jean-Claude Servais, the Gaume in comics
culture.text: The comic-book artist Jean-Claude Servais (born 1956) lives in Jamoigne, next to Izel. His albums draw on the landscapes, witchcraft and legends of the Gaume and the Ardennes: La Tchalette (1982), Tendre Violette, and Orval in two volumes published by Dupuis, on the history of the abbey. His artwork was exhibited in Bastogne in 2025.

culture.title: The Herbeumont slate quarries
culture.text: The monks of Orval and Saint-Hubert were already quarrying slate in the Herbeumont forests in the 13th century. The industry boomed in the 1830s, with around 8 million slates a year by about 1838. The blue-grey roofs of the valley come from here. You can learn more at the Au cœur de l'Ardoise museum in Bertrix, opened in 1996 in the former Morépire slate quarry.

culture.title: The Priory of Conques
culture.text: A former house of studies of Orval Abbey, on the banks of the Semois about 2 km south of Herbeumont. It has been a hotel since 1963.

culture.title: Semois tobacco, intangible heritage
culture.text: In the lower Semois valley (Vresse, Bohan, Laforêt, Corbion), tobacco has been grown since the 1850s. Wooden drying sheds can still be seen, and two waymarked loops form the Route du tabac (Tobacco Route). The know-how was recognised as intangible cultural heritage of the Wallonia-Brussels Federation at the end of 2024, but only a handful of growers remain. These villages are about 40 km downstream from Izel.

culture.title: Torgny, Belgium's southernmost village
culture.text: A village of pale golden stone, listed among the Most Beautiful Villages of Wallonia, with its terraced vineyards, St Martin's Church, the Notre-Dame chapel and its hermitage. It is the very picture of the Gaume's “little Provence”.
